comparator.name: Aardwetenschappen (Earth Sciences)
comparator.sourceNotes: The current Utrecht programme is a 180-EC three-year bachelor. Year one is a fixed broad Earth Sciences foundation: six ordinary 7.5-EC courses and 15 EC of Fieldwork 1. From year two the programme has four formal specialisations. No one specialisation is identified as uniquely primary; Vorming van het aardoppervlak is first in the official current curriculum and is selected by the neutral official-order tie-break. Its year-two structure contains six 7.5-EC taught courses plus two 7.5-EC Fieldwork 2 modules. Where alternatives exist, the first option in official order is selected: Data Analysis and Statistics, Delta Evolution and Subsurface, Coastal and River Dynamics, and the Italy/lowland-genesis fieldwork pairing. Year three contains the compulsory 15-EC Earth Sciences bachelor thesis and 45 EC of genuine elective, minor or study-abroad space. All components total exactly 180 EC.

routeSelection.basis: The normalized target is the generic Earth Sciences bachelor. Utrecht lists four equally formal specialisations and does not identify one as the general route. Vorming van het aardoppervlak appears first in the current official curriculum, so it is selected by neutral official order independently of UCR fit. Within that route, official order also resolves the published choices.

core: Earth as a dynamic system: deep-Earth, lithosphere, surface, water, climate and life interactions
Physical and chemical Earth processes, geology, geochemistry, geophysics, hydrology and climate processes
Quantitative Earth science through mathematics, statistics, scientific programming, GIS, modelling and evidence
Surface formation through geomorphology, water flow, Earth observation, delta evolution and coastal and river dynamics
Field observation, laboratory analysis, mapping and interpretation
Independent Earth Sciences research and bachelor thesis
adjacent: Climate change, natural hazards, adaptation and changing landscapes
Groundwater, surface water, soils, deltas and sustainable water management
Sustainability, resources, environmental change and human influence on Earth systems
questions: How do interacting physical, chemical and biological processes form and change Earth's surface?
How do water, climate and human intervention reshape landscapes, deltas and environmental risk?

candidates.label: Educational minor for geography, physics or chemistry teaching
candidates.reason: UCR can study Earth systems and related sciences but does not provide subject-didactics courses, supervised secondary-school teaching practice or the formal teacher-qualification sequence needed to make a coherent education-focused 24-course alternative.

alternatives.label: Earth systems, water and surface processes
alternatives.concept: Combines Earth science, Earth-system modelling, climate, hazards, soils, aquifers, water and delta processes with GIS, field- and lab-oriented environmental study, mathematics, statistics and data methods. It is the closest feasible UCR response to the selected surface-formation route while preserving UCR's lack of a full geology, mineralogy, palaeontology and geophysics sequence.
progression: Dynamic Earth, Sustainability Essentials I and introductory data study precede Earth-system tools, advanced sustainability and GIS. Mathematical Methods precedes Linear Algebra, Numerical Methods and Probability & Statistics. The two sustainability gateways precede all courses that formally require them; all term offerings pass.
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum is dominated by Earth-system science, surface and water processes, climate, spatial evidence and quantitative methods; the label does not imply the missing full geological-specialist sequence.

selection.assessment: One strong 24-course Earth-systems programme is feasible. The only generator-eligible direction outside the core is the formal educational minor, but UCR lacks subject didactics, supervised school practice and teacher qualification. Water, climate and hazards are already major organising strands of the closest curriculum; splitting them off would largely reshuffle the same environmental-science courses rather than produce a genuinely different programme.

blocks: Earth systems, geology, chemistry and life
Both introduce interacting deep-Earth, lithosphere, hydrosphere and surface processes; Utrecht additionally has systematic mineral, fossil and geological-structure identification.
Both treat Earth as an interacting system and use evidence about past and future conditions; Utrecht places evolution and geological history more centrally.
Both examine chemical equilibria, minerals and water-rock interactions; Utrecht also supplies a broader chemistry and isotope-geology foundation.
Both address the subsurface and its use; Utrecht reconstructs Dutch stratigraphy and geological development, while UCR focuses on contemporary resources and storage.
Utrecht's dedicated geomorphology course has no single UCR course counterpart.
Utrecht's compulsory 15-EC geological fieldwork sequence remains unmatched by one ordinary UCR course.
Surface processes, water, climate and environmental change
Both analyse coastal and river processes in relation to floods and land use; UCR emphasises nature-based engineering applications.
Both use GIS and remotely sensed Earth data for spatial environmental analysis.
Both examine groundwater and surface-water processes; UCR combines aquifer mapping with soils and resource applications.
Both study delta evolution, subsidence and water dynamics; UCR emphasises present-day adaptation and management.
Utrecht's route-specific source-to-sink field module has no ordinary UCR course equivalent.
Utrecht's route-specific lowland-genesis field module has no ordinary UCR course equivalent.
Both develop computational work with scientific data; Utrecht additionally teaches the physics of internal and surface Earth processes.
Both provide calculus and mathematical foundations; Utrecht integrates introductory statistics and Earth-science applications.
Both develop statistical analysis for scientific data; UCR adds probability theory and simulation.
Applied work, research and elective space
Both require substantive environmental research and reporting; Utrecht's component is an individual 15-EC Earth Sciences thesis, while UCR's is a team project with an external partner.
The genuine 45-EC elective, minor or study-abroad space remains open and is not assigned invented Earth Sciences content.

notes.text: Both programmes include substantial study of Earth systems, climate, water, soils, hazards, GIS, geochemistry and quantitative environmental evidence. Utrecht additionally requires a deeper geological foundation in rocks, minerals, fossils, stratigraphy, geomorphology and long fieldwork sequences. UCR instead combines the available Earth-science core with sustainability, delta studies, ecology and quantitative methods; it does not reproduce the full specialist geology curriculum.
